Background and Objectives Multiple sclerosis (MS), neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD), and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody–associated disease (MOGAD) are autoimmune disorders of the CNS causing severe neurologic impairment. Evidence suggests that extracellular vesicles (EVs) may play a disease-specific role in the orchestration of the immune cell response of MS, NMOSD, and MOGAD. In addition, EVs are considered as a potential source of biomarkers that may allow us to establish molecular signatures for these diseases and perhaps as well to follow treatment effects and disease progression. The aim of this study was to analyze the composition of EVs in patients with relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS) (n = 52), NMOSD (n = 19), and MOGAD (n = 10) and healthy controls ([HCs], n = 15). Methods The concentrations of neurofilament light chain (NfL) and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) were determined in plasma using single-molecule array (SIMOA). The size and concentration of tetraspanin-presenting EVs were evaluated in plasma samples with a single-particle interferometric resonance imaging sensor (SP-IRIS). Tetraspanin-independent analyses were performed by nanoparticle-tracking analysis (NTA) after EV isolation by size exclusion (SmartSEC) and cryo-electron microscopy observations. EV epitopes were analyzed by extended multiplex analysis using flow cytometry. Results The plasma concentration of NfL and GFAP was significantly higher in patients with RRMS than in HCs. For patients with NMOSD, only GFAP increased. The density of EVs assessed by NTA was lower in plasma of patients with RRMS than in HC plasma. In addition, the 3 disease groups presented increased mean EV sizes in comparison with HCs. Tetraspanin-based EV analyses by SP-IRIS allowed us to observe a modest difference in the level of CD81 in RRMS EVs. In patients with RRMS, but not in those with NMOSD and MOGAD, multiplex/flow cytometry analyses revealed changes in the EV levels of CD29, CD31, and CD69 associated with the time elapsed since the last relapse. The negative correlations established between the vesicular levels of CD31, CD40, CD44, CD49c, CD69, and NfL or GFAP z-scores suggest a negative relationship specifically in RRMS. Discussion We speculate that the higher release of EVs containing CD29, CD31, CD40, CD44, CD49c, and CD69 in plasma, at low levels of circulating NfL/GFAP, may be associated with reduced immune cell activity in RRMS. These EV markers may characterize patients with RRMS in disease stabilization. OPEN-ACCESS TRUE Introduction Multiple sclerosis (MS), neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD), and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody–associated disease (MOGAD) are chronic autoimmune demyelinating diseases of the CNS. They present overlapping motor, sensory, and cognitive symptoms, such as vision and walking impairment, respectively, caused by optic nerve and spinal cord lesions. 1 In contrast to MS, where no specific autoantibody profile has been established, current diagnosis of NMOSD and MOGAD heavily relies on serum autoantibodies. 2,3 Although AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG greatly facilitate diagnosis, their blood concentrations do not correlate with disease activity or treatment effects. By contrast, the serum levels of neurofilament light chain (NfL) and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), reflecting neuronal damage and MS progression, respectively, have been linked to disease activity. 4,5 However, these molecules are not disease-specific. 6,7 Therefore, more sensitive and specific tools are required for improving diagnosis and follow-up of disease course. In recent years, cell-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as a promising source of disease biomarkers in blood and CSF. 8,9 EVs are small bilayered membranous particles ranging between approximately 50 and 1,000 nm in diameter. By delivering proteins, lipids, and mRNA, EVs contribute to the intercellular communication. 10 In the immune system, cytokines, chemokines, coagulation factors, and antigens enclosed in T-cell–shed EVs are important mediators between the innate and adaptive immune response. 11,12 Notably, high levels of T-cell–derived EVs in serum and CSF are associated with MS relapse. 13,14 Whether immune cells release EVs in different amounts and of different compositions in MS, NMOSD, and MOGAD is not known. Moreover, CNS cells also secrete EVs in MS; myelin-specific proteins, such as myelin basic protein (MBP) and MOG, have been detected in EVs isolated from the plasma and CSF of patients with MS, suggesting that oligodendrocyte-shed EVs cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and reach the circulation. 15 In addition, the level of MBP-positive and MOG-positive EVs correlated with disability measured using Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) scores. 16,17 Very little is known about the protein cargoes of EVs in NMOSD and MOGAD. In NMOSD relapse, astrocytes release specific microRNAs (miRNAs) encapsulated in EVs that are detectable in the blood. 18,19 Importantly, the authors showed that some of these miRNAs induced demyelinating lesions in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo. 19 At the protein level, it has been suggested that GFAP and complement factor C4b-binding protein α-chain may be enriched in CSF-derived EVs in patients with NMOSD compared with MS, but further investigations are necessary to confirm these observations. 20 Comparative analyses in MS vs NMOSD vs MOGAD are missing to determine whether EV proteins differ in a disease-specific fashion. The aim of this study was to characterize circulating EVs in patients with MS, NMOSD, and MOGAD in parallel. It is important to underline that EVs are heterogeneous particles, of variable sizes and cellular origins, resulting from different biogenesis mechanisms (cell membrane budding and fusion of multivesicular endosomes). Therefore, throughout this study, the nonrestrictive term “EVs” encompassing all categories of vesicles was preferred, as recommended by the International Society of Extracellular Vesicles and the MISEV2023 Guidelines. 21 In the membrane of EVs, CD9, CD63, and CD81 tetraspanins are considered as specific markers. 22 Nevertheless, the level of tetraspanins varies between cell types, tissues, and diseases. 23 For this reason, tetraspanin-dependent and independent methods were used to examine EVs. An extended analysis of 37 EV epitopes revealed specific enrichments in MS samples by flow cytometry.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study aimed to characterize circulating extracellular vesicles (EVs), neurofilament light chain (NfL), and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) in the plasma of patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS), neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD), and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) compared to healthy controls. Key findings include significantly higher plasma NfL and GFAP in RRMS patients, with GFAP also elevated in NMOSD patients. RRMS patients exhibited lower EV density and increased mean EV size compared to controls, with larger EVs (>150nm) primarily contributing to this. Furthermore, specific EV surface markers (CD29, CD31, CD40, CD44, CD49c, CD69) showed changes in RRMS patients, notably correlating negatively with NfL/GFAP levels and positively with time since the last relapse, suggesting their potential as biomarkers for disease stabilization and reduced immune cell activity, independent of current treatments.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study characterizing biomarkers in patients with Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis (RRMS), Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD), and Myelin Oligodendrocyte Glycoprotein Antibody-Associated Disease (MOGAD) undergoing existing pharmacological treatments.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study included 96 participants (52 RRMS, 19 NMOSD, 10 MOGAD, 15 healthy controls). RRMS patients received natalizumab (n=33), dimethylfumarate/glatiramer acetate (n=12), or no treatment (n=7). NMOSD patients were treated with rituximab, and MOGAD patients had various heterogeneous treatments. While existing treatments were noted, no specific therapeutic interventions or dose comparisons were investigated by the study itself. Biomarker measurements were performed using SIMOA, SP-IRIS, cryo-EM, Western blotting, NTA, and multiplex flow cytometry. The study concluded that current treatments did not significantly influence the observed EV marker levels or composition.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly higher in patients with Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis (RRMS) than in healthy controls (HCs) (Figure 2, A and B), suggesting prominent axonal damage. No significant difference for NfL z-score between RRMS, NMOSD, and MOGAD groups (Figure 2A). NfL z-scores were adjusted for age based on a large reference cohort.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Structural protein of neurons, released into circulation following Central Nervous System (CNS) neuronal damage.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: CNS neuron damage and disease activity in Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis (RRMS), Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD), and Myelin Oligodendrocyte Glycoprotein Antibody-Associated Disease (MOGAD).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Considered a potential surrogate biomarker of neuronal damage and disease activity in demyelinating diseases of the CNS, indicating prominent axonal damage in RRMS. Useful for following disease activity and linked to a negative correlation with certain EV markers in RRMS, suggesting an association with low disease activity.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly higher in patients with Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis (RRMS) than in healthy controls (HCs) (Figure 2, A and B), suggesting gliosis. A significant increase in NMOSD compared with HCs (Figure 2B) indicates astrocytopathy. No significant difference for GFAP z-score between RRMS, NMOSD, and MOGAD groups (Figure 2A). Preliminary GFAP z-scores were adjusted for age and sex based on a large reference database.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Intermediate filament protein in astrocytes, released into circulation after astrogliosis (astrocytic damage/injury response) in the CNS.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Astrocytic injury/response and disease activity in the CNS of patients with Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis (RRMS) and Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD), but not Myelin Oligodendrocyte Glycoprotein Antibody-Associated Disease (MOGAD).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Considered a potential surrogate biomarker of astrogliosis and disease activity in demyelinating diseases of the CNS, indicating gliosis in RRMS and astrocytopathy in NMOSD. Useful for following disease activity and linked to a negative correlation with certain EV markers in RRMS, suggesting an association with low disease activity.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower concentrations of EVs in the Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis (RRMS) group than in healthy controls (HCs) when assessed by Nanoparticle-tracking analysis (NTA) (Figure 4B). However, EV concentration was similar between disease groups when measured by Single-particle interferometric resonance imaging sensor (SP-IRIS).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicates the quantity of extracellular vesicles, reflecting mechanisms controlling microparticle and exosome shedding and mediating intercellular communication.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis (RRMS) disease activity compared to Healthy Controls (HCs).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: May reflect altered mechanisms controlling nonselective microparticle and exosome shedding in RRMS and is associated with the disease state.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Mean EV size did not vary between the 3 disease groups (123.1 nm in RRMS; 114.3 nm in NMOSD, and 117.2 nm in MOGAD) but was significantly bigger than that of HCs (96.3 nm) (Figure 4C). Particle size distribution analysis suggests EVs larger than 150 nm predominantly contribute to this effect. Peak size distribution was at 76.5 nm in RRMS, 77.5 nm in NMOSD, 76.5 nm in MOGAD, and 72.5 nm in HCs. The size of tetraspanin-labeled EVs did not differ significantly between disease groups.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Physical characteristic of EVs, related to EV subtypes (e.g., exosomes vs. microparticles) and underlying biogenesis mechanisms, mediating intercellular communication.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis (RRMS), Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD), Myelin Oligodendrocyte Glycoprotein Antibody-Associated Disease (MOGAD) disease activity compared to Healthy Controls (HCs).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: May reflect altered EV biogenesis mechanisms or involvement of larger EV subtypes (e.g., microparticles > 150 nm) in these autoimmune disorders, and is associated with their respective disease states.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: A modest difference in the level of CD81 was observed in Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis (RRMS) EVs through tetraspanin-based EV analyses by SP-IRIS. Specifically, fluorescence intensity of the CD81 signal for EVs captured with CD63 and CD9 was lower in patients with RRMS than in the two other disease groups (NMOSD and MOGAD).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: CD81 is a tetraspanin, a common EV membrane marker involved in cell adhesion, motility, migration, and signal transduction. Also involved in enabling EV capture and characterization.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis (RRMS) disease activity compared to Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD) and Myelin Oligodendrocyte Glycoprotein Antibody-Associated Disease (MOGAD).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Potentially indicates specific EV subpopulations or altered EV characteristics and composition in RRMS, useful for identification, capture, and subcategorization of EVs.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Levels significantly changed in patients with RRMS along with the time elapsed since the last relapse (positively associated) and NfL or GFAP z-scores. Speculated to be 'higher release' in plasma at low levels of circulating NfL/GFAP. Levels of this EV marker did not significantly differ between the whole groups (RRMS, NMOSD, MOGAD).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: CD29 (Integrin beta-1) is involved in cell adhesion and signaling, and leukocyte trafficking. It is a T-cell and leukocyte-associated marker.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis (RRMS) disease activity, specifically associated with time since last relapse and inversely correlated with NfL/GFAP levels.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: May characterize patients with RRMS in disease stabilization and be associated with reduced immune cell activity. Increased expression may be associated with low disease activity.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Levels significantly changed in patients with RRMS, positively associated with time since the last relapse. A negative correlation was established between CD31 levels and plasma NfL or GFAP z-scores specifically in RRMS. A decline was observed for increasing concentrations of NfL. Conversely, increased levels were observed at low NfL and GFAP concentrations. Speculated to be 'higher release' in plasma at low levels of circulating NfL/GFAP. Levels of this EV marker did not significantly differ between the whole groups (RRMS, NMOSD, MOGAD).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: CD31 (PECAM-1) is involved in cell adhesion, leukocyte transendothelial migration, and blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability. Its release via EVs may induce cell loss of function or reflect an attempt at restoring BBB integrity.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis (RRMS) disease activity and post-relapse remission.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: May characterize patients with RRMS in disease stabilization and be associated with reduced immune cell activity. Lower levels are associated with higher NfL (higher disease activity) in RRMS. Higher levels are associated with remission and low NfL/GFAP, potentially reflecting an attempt to restore BBB integrity or a mechanism reducing CNS infiltration by immune cells.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Levels significantly changed in patients with RRMS, positively associated with time since the last relapse. A negative correlation was established between CD69 levels and plasma NfL or GFAP z-scores specifically in RRMS. A decline was observed for increasing concentrations of NfL. Lower levels were associated with higher concentrations of GFAP. Conversely, increased levels were observed with the time elapsed since the last relapse and were higher when NfL and/or GFAP levels were relatively low. Speculated to be 'higher release' in plasma at low levels of circulating NfL/GFAP. Levels of this EV marker did not significantly differ between the whole groups (RRMS, NMOSD, MOGAD).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: CD69 is an early activation marker for lymphocytes. Highly expressed in T cells of active MS lesions. In EVs, its potential removal may reduce leukocyte activation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis (RRMS) disease activity and post-relapse remission.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: May characterize patients with RRMS in disease stabilization and be associated with reduced immune cell activity. Lower levels are associated with higher NfL and GFAP (higher disease activity) in RRMS. Higher levels are associated with remission and low NfL/GFAP, potentially indicating a mechanism reducing leukocyte activation in the periphery.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Levels significantly changed in patients with RRMS along with NfL or GFAP z-scores. Speculated to be 'higher release' in plasma at low levels of circulating NfL/GFAP. Levels of this EV marker did not significantly differ between the whole groups (RRMS, NMOSD, MOGAD).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: CD40 is a costimulatory molecule on antigen-presenting cells, important for immune responses, and dampens cell differentiation. In EVs, its potential removal from the cell surface may dampen immune response.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis (RRMS) disease activity, inversely correlated with NfL/GFAP z-scores.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: May characterize patients with RRMS in disease stabilization and be associated with reduced immune cell activity. Lower levels are associated with higher NfL (higher disease activity) in RRMS. Potential removal of CD40 from the surface of antigen-presenting cells via EV shedding may dampen cell differentiation and regulate immune response.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Levels significantly changed in patients with RRMS along with NfL or GFAP z-scores. A negative correlation was established between CD44 levels and plasma NfL specifically in RRMS. A decline was observed for increasing concentrations of NfL. Lower levels were associated with higher concentrations of GFAP. Conversely, increased levels were observed at low NfL and GFAP concentrations. Speculated to be 'higher release' in plasma at low levels of circulating NfL/GFAP. Levels of this EV marker did not significantly differ between the whole groups (RRMS, NMOSD, MOGAD).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: CD44 is a cell surface glycoprotein involved in cell-cell adhesion, cell migration, and lymphocyte activation. Highly expressed in T cells of active MS lesions. In EVs, its potential removal may reduce leukocyte activation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis (RRMS) disease activity, inversely correlated with NfL/GFAP z-scores.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: May characterize patients with RRMS in disease stabilization and be associated with reduced immune cell activity. Lower levels are associated with higher NfL and GFAP (higher disease activity) in RRMS. Higher levels are associated with weak disease activity, potentially indicating a mechanism reducing leukocyte activation in the periphery or protection of the BBB.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: CD49c (Integrin alpha-3) is involved in cell adhesion to extracellular matrix, cell signaling, and leukocyte extravasation. In EVs, its potential removal may reduce central nervous system (CNS) infiltration.

analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: May characterize patients with RRMS in disease stabilization and be associated with reduced immune cell activity. measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Detection of Alix was performed as an intravesicular marker, but no quantitative data on its level or change are provided; it serves as a general EV marker.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Intravesicular marker, commonly used to characterize and confirm the presence of extracellular vesicles.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Characterization of plasma EVs in patients with RRMS, AQP4-positive NMOSD, MOG-positive MOGAD, and healthy controls.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Cutoffs were set for SP-IRIS to obtain average counts of <50 for CD63/CD81 and <100 for CD9. For flow cytometry, median signal intensities were measured. No quantitative changes in expression levels specifically for CD9 or CD63 were reported as disease-specific effects, primarily used for EV characterization.
